title: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Nick Fleisher

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Fleisher does not develop the cluster’s claim that automation threatens the reproduction of associate expertise. He instead argues that current AI is not a like-for-like substitute for junior lawyers and prioritises automating in-house administrative work while lawyers retain substantive judgment.
qs: I would push back and say everyone should really focus on spending their time doing the real, deep legal work and let the AI, as much as possible, take care of the admin things.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The excerpt only introduces Sandstone as an AI platform for in-house legal teams using business-wide context. It provides no substantive view on dispute-resolution access, AI-assisted versus autonomous adjudication, safeguards, legitimacy, or performance evidence, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.
qs: But I'm thrilled to have with us Nick Fleisher, who is the co-founder and CEO of Sandstone, which is an AI-native platform built specifically for in-house legal teams.
Sandstone uses AI to pull in context from across the business, not just within the legal department.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Fleisher accepts the central proposition that in-house legal technology should improve business-to-legal coordination rather than merely store or review contracts. He materially develops it through a concrete platform model combining intake, deal context, prior negotiations and a cross-system knowledge graph, while offering ambitions and qualitative observations rather than measured outcomes.
qs: And there was no in-between that said: Let's tackle the actual issue around how people in the business interact with legal.

And let's build a platform that doesn't just connect contracts to counterparties, but rather every document to every person, to every company, so that when we're actually using AI, we always can surface the right context immediately.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Fleisher accepts the cluster’s core view that in-house adoption should redesign delivery around business outcomes, integrated context and risk-based human oversight. He materially extends it with a proactive operating model in which AI monitors business systems to anticipate legal bottlenecks and informs preparatory work or staffing, while leaving consequential judgment to lawyers. His observations that outside-counsel time and cost have not visibly changed also reinforce the cluster’s caution about current evidence.
qs: But I think, more importantly, if you adopt AI well on the in-house side, your legal team becomes more proactive rather than reactive.
But when we get to much more high-stakes, high-value work, that's where, from an ROI perspective, you still want a human making those final judgment calls.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Fleisher reinforces the treatment of in-house legal departments as distinct AI customers and materially develops the product-market rationale: effective tools should gather business and counterparty context and consolidate fragmented departmental knowledge. His account supports stronger internal capability but does not itself establish reduced outside-counsel use.
qs: The tool has already gone back and forth with the sales rep to understand all the context on the deal that matters, and the tool will go pull all your past contracts and negotiations with that counterparty.
And we want to consolidate that into a single knowledge-layer context graph that is kind of the source of truth for your legal department.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Fleisher materially develops the cluster’s core proposition by specifying an in-house legal workflow layer: a context graph connecting documents, people and companies, then using retrieved deal history to support drafting and review. His account also reinforces the importance of organisational workflow fit, though it remains a product vision without measured performance or explicit verification evidence.
qs: And let's build a platform that doesn't just connect contracts to counterparties, but rather every document to every person, to every company, so that when we're actually using AI, we always can surface the right context immediately.
It then takes that context and uses it to help you either draft an answer, review an agreement, or draft a contract.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts practitioner-led experimentation and materially develops the cluster’s implementation case by specifying business-context inputs, embedded former lawyers and legal-operations experts, and practical user education. It offers an operational model for shared adoption, while not demonstrating comparative effectiveness or reliable outcomes.
qs: That's where implementation and having folks who understand the implications of the inputs that you give the tool is just super important.

We partner with LECG, but we partner with many others, and we have a big function internally, which is largely former lawyers as well as former heads of legal ops who have seen these challenges before and can embed themselves in organizations and understand what's actually helpful here, and how do we make sure that people are using the things properly.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Fleisher accepts that AI value depends on institutional implementation rather than access alone and materially develops the proposition for in-house legal departments: use-case-specific data, cross-system context, gradual workflow learning, embedded legal expertise and risk-sensitive human controls. His account also reinforces the cluster’s caution that current adoption has not demonstrated broad cost or productivity gains.
qs: If you don't have your data in order, and you don't have the right context to pull from, the AI is not going to look very different from what happens if you ask ChatGPT or Claude.

We partner with LECG, but we partner with many others, and we have a big function internally, which is largely former lawyers as well as former heads of legal ops who have seen these challenges before and can embed themselves in organizations and understand what's actually helpful here, and how do we make sure that people are using the things properly.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source accepts the engagement-first proposition and materially develops its implementation dimension by specifying embedded former lawyers and legal operations leaders, input-aware deployment, and office-hours training as practical adoption supports. It also links that support prospectively to higher-value work, while offering no measured evidence of effectiveness.
qs: We partner with LECG, but we partner with many others, and we have a big function internally, which is largely former lawyers as well as former heads of legal ops who have seen these challenges before and can embed themselves in organizations and understand what's actually helpful here, and how do we make sure that people are using the things properly.
We do a lot of office hours, just teaching people what works and what doesn't.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core copilot model: AI should automate bounded administrative and context-gathering tasks while lawyers retain review and final business-risk judgment. It materially extends the synthesis by framing proactive, cross-system anticipation of in-house legal needs—and AI-generated increases in demand—as important consequences beyond straightforward production efficiency.
qs: But I think, more importantly, if you adopt AI well on the in-house side, your legal team becomes more proactive rather than reactive.

If you have an agent that can send a Slack to someone to gather context and then take that and use it to improve a redline, that’s totally fine as long as that person you’re Slacking was expecting the message and you’re still signing off and reviewing the redline.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI is organisational redesign rather than a stand-alone software purchase and materially develops the proposition with a concrete implementation model: use-case-specific data integration, embedded legal and legal-operations expertise, iterative learning from workflows, user education, and risk-tiered human approval. Its claims are based mainly on implementation experience rather than quantified outcomes.
qs: You really have to think about each use case and what type of data you need and where that data lives.

We partner with LECG, but we partner with many others, and we have a big function internally, which is largely former lawyers as well as former heads of legal ops who have seen these challenges before and can embed themselves in organizations and understand what's actually helpful here, and how do we make sure that people are using the things properly.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Fleisher accepts the cluster’s core view that AI should selectively reorganise work around retained human judgment, not replace lawyers wholesale. He materially extends it with a concrete in-house operating model: prioritise intake, triage, context gathering and cross-system data integration before complex legal tasks, while reserving high-stakes final decisions for lawyers.
qs: Nick Fleisher: As we've talked about, a lot of the benefits of building a more proactive legal department using agents are on things that are not necessarily the raw legal judgment, but rather all the things around it that get you to the point where you need to come to a decision around something that is legal-related.
But when we get to much more high-stakes, high-value work, that's where, from an ROI perspective, you still want a human making those final judgment calls.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Fleisher supports the cluster’s core account of agentic legal AI as multistep, cross-system delegation whose autonomy varies and whose human checkpoints should increase with risk. He also reinforces the cluster’s caution that implementation depends on workflow change and data preparation, while current evidence does not justify autonomous end-to-end practice or like-for-like staffing reductions.
qs: I think people generally think agent means autonomous, but it may not mean that.
I think in those, you want to see more human-in-the-loop steps, where you have to press approve on anything that the agent is going to go do.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of agentic legal work as connected, context-aware workflows with retained human checkpoints rather than fully autonomous replacement. It adds risk-based examples for in-house teams, while offering only host framing—not substantive evidence—on transferring institutional knowledge into workflows.
qs: If you have an agent that can send a Slack to someone to gather context and then take that and use it to improve a redline, that’s totally fine as long as that person you’re Slacking was expecting the message and you’re still signing off and reviewing the redline.

I think we are a very long way out, if not completely out, from in-house teams having fully autonomous tools that are going and completing end-to-end workflows without them touching them or being a human in the loop.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central account of unevenly realised AI gains and growing buyer-side pressure. It reports that in-house teams face faster-turnaround expectations while outside counsel’s claimed AI use has not yet produced visible reductions in delivery time, billed hours or total cost. These are conversational observations rather than quantified market-wide evidence.
qs: So lawyers are now expected to turn things around faster.

Then, turning to the law firms and outside counsel, most GCs I talk to say that they ask their outside counsel about AI usage, and they say they’re using it, but they don’t see any change in either delivery times or actual billed hours and total cost.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Fleisher supports the cluster’s cautious, task-specific account: current AI is not a like-for-like staff substitute, consequential legal judgment remains human, and agentic workflows should retain review and sign-off. He also reinforces the possibility that expanded demand may absorb capacity gains. However, he does not directly address apprenticeship, partner succession, explicit training funding or broader career paths.
qs: If you have an agent that can send a Slack to someone to gather context and then take that and use it to improve a redline, that’s totally fine as long as that person you’re Slacking was expecting the message and you’re still signing off and reviewing the redline.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that legal AI value depends on implementation, legal-context expertise and sustained user training rather than model capability alone. It links poor upfront implementation to weaker outputs and trust, and describes embedded former lawyers and legal-operations leaders as practical adoption support; its claims remain experience-based rather than measured outcome evidence.
qs: That's where implementation and having folks who understand the implications of the inputs that you give the tool is just super important.

We partner with LECG, but we partner with many others, and we have a big function internally, which is largely former lawyers as well as former heads of legal ops who have seen these challenges before and can embed themselves in organizations and understand what's actually helpful here, and how do we make sure that people are using the things properly.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Fleisher supports the cluster’s core view that AI can expand capacity without independently transforming access. He favors automation for some otherwise unaddressed low-value work, but retains lawyers for final judgment and frames staffing and task-allocation changes as necessary to realize AI’s benefits.
qs: And so I do think that there will always be some level of last-mile decision-making that lawyers will be making, and we're not going to fully automate that.

Let's either deploy AI to help prep work or get on the low-level stuff, or we actually need to change how we think about staffing and our team."  I think that's the real promise of AI: if you can get to the point where it's spotting things before they happen so that we're actually able to move faster and buy ourselves more time.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Fleisher supports the cluster’s core task-substitution and complementarity proposition: some low-stakes legal work may be fully automated, while lawyers retain final judgment for higher-stakes matters. His account is qualitative and does not establish broader staffing or employment effects.
qs: I do think there's a world where AI can fully automate some of it.
But when we get to much more high-stakes, high-value work, that's where, from an ROI perspective, you still want a human making those final judgment calls.

kp.k: Integrated context underpins in-house workflow automation
kp.d: Fleisher describes Sandstone as centralizing requests from business systems, routing them within legal, gathering commercial context and prior counterparty dealings, and assisting drafting and review. This is a vendor's account of product capabilities and its intended evolving knowledge layer, rather than an independently measured productivity finding.
qs: Sandstone helps in-house legal teams manage intake, work execution, triage, and knowledge across their department.
It then takes that context and uses it to help you either draft an answer, review an agreement, or draft a contract.
And we want to consolidate that into a single knowledge-layer context graph that is kind of the source of truth for your legal department.

kp.k: Organizational alignment shapes adoption more than tool availability
kp.d: Drawing on his consulting experience, Fleisher says law firms adopted AI earlier because they could spend on immature tools, but achieving common workflows across large partnerships was difficult. He contrasts this with the potential for aligned in-house teams to adopt shared infrastructure, and identifies a gap between contract repositories, redlining tools and business-facing intake. Engineering tools such as Linear and Jira provide his organizational analogy.
qs: it's very hard to convince 2,000 Big Law partners to go use the same infrastructure and the same workflows.

Then with my in-house clients, it felt like if you got them aligned on one vision or one way of working, there was real opportunity for upside where everyone could leverage something that would be valuable.
So we learned a lot from how engineering teams work and engage with the rest of the company, and wanted to bring that to legal.

kp.k: Data readiness precedes effective legal AI deployment
kp.d: Fleisher argues that relevant, organized data is foundational across legal services, not merely an implementation detail after deploying a chatbot. He considers the challenge especially pronounced in-house because relevant information spans business systems rather than residing solely in a document management system. His recommendation is to map each use case's data requirements and locations.
qs: One is that most organizations don't realize that the core of getting AI right is just a data problem.
You really have to think about each use case and what type of data you need and where that data lives.
I think it's most pronounced in-house because the data typically doesn't just live in a DMS like in law firms.

kp.k: AI could make legal departments proactive
kp.d: Beyond cost savings, Fleisher identifies anticipation of demand and capacity bottlenecks as AI's promise. He says some clients use tools monitoring business systems to identify impending legal work, allowing preparation, lower-level automation or staffing adjustments before legal delays arise. This combines reported client practice with a forward-looking account of value; no measured results are supplied.
qs: if you adopt AI well on the in-house side, your legal team becomes more proactive rather than reactive.

With AI, what we see some of our clients doing is you have a bot or a tool that lives on top of Slack or on top of Salesforce or your procurement tool or even on top of Jira, and it starts to spot things before they happen.
I think that's the real promise of AI: if you can get to the point where it's spotting things before they happen so that we're actually able to move faster and buy ourselves more time.

kp.k: Institutional preferences require observation and iterative feedback
kp.d: Fleisher acknowledges that initial integrations and historical material do not fully capture lawyers' judgment or preferences. He describes observing manual routing, approvals and information selection during the first couple of weeks, then learning from use and feedback. Comparing individual and team practices may expose habitual clause choices or unsupported assumptions about counterparties' bargaining power; he frames these as decision differences, not exclusively social-equity bias.
qs: the first couple of things you do are not going to feel like you. There's still going to be a gap.

Usually, for the first couple of weeks of using the tool, we can actually ask you to do that manually the same way you do today, but do it while our tool is there on top of Teams or Slack or Word or email.

But the more common one would be routinely falling back to a certain provision or clause that the rest of the company doesn't, or that is not market standard, just because it's something that you've done so many times over.
Maybe it's not actually thinking about it in terms of decision bias, but rather decision correctness or decision difference to the mean of what the rest of your peers are doing.

kp.k: Prioritize administrative automation over complex legal redlining
kp.d: Fleisher rejects the host's broad characterization of lawyers as stubborn, defending scrutiny of rapidly funded AI products. He nevertheless reports resistance to relinquishing administrative decisions and recommends automating intake, assignment and information retrieval before targeting difficult substantive work such as redlining. The intended role change is greater concentration on deep legal work.
qs: I think everyone has the right to be stubborn and to push back and to ask questions.
I would push back and say everyone should really focus on spending their time doing the real, deep legal work and let the AI, as much as possible, take care of the admin things.

I think we've jumped too quickly to saying, "Let's go build and do AI redlining," which is one of the more complex parts of the day-to-day of many commercial in-house lawyers, versus: What about all the triaging and managing who's doing what work?

kp.k: Human judgment remains central, with limited automation exceptions
kp.d: Fleisher predicts that lawyers will retain final decisions balancing business outcomes against legal risk, particularly in high-stakes work. He distinguishes AI presenting considerations from accurately deciding between them. He allows that some low-volume or low-stakes work, including lowest-value arbitration cases that might otherwise not be addressed, could be fully automated where the cost tradeoff warrants it.
qs: AI can give you both sides, but for it to accurately make the decision is hard.
And so I do think that there will always be some level of last-mile decision-making that lawyers will be making, and we're not going to fully automate that.
Now, in some low-volume or low-stakes work, I think we can start to automate it. You see this in the lowest-value arbitration cases.
But when we get to much more high-stakes, high-value work, that's where, from an ROI perspective, you still want a human making those final judgment calls.

kp.k: AI-generated business activity can increase legal workload
kp.d: Fleisher argues that AI increases agreements, transactions and material requiring legal attention, including poorly prepared inputs. He relays one GC's estimate of 30 to 40% more work, not a systematic workload study, and predicts further growth. Separately, McCormack asserts that courts are seeing more filings from both lawyers and people unable to afford them, including more motions and pages per motion.
qs: Because of AI, we see organizations are doing a lot more. They’re generating a lot more agreements. They’re negotiating more things. They’re buying more stuff.

I was talking to a GC the other day and they were like, “Honestly, we’re probably seeing 30 to 40% more work just because of how much sloppier the things are that are coming out of product and procurement and all these different places because everything’s AI-generated.”

The courts are seeing increased filings, not only from people who can’t afford lawyers, but also from lawyers. Lawyers are just filing significantly more motions and significantly more pages per motion, and it’s AI in the background in both places.

kp.k: Proactive practice requires delegating information gathering
kp.d: Fleisher says lawyers will need to rely on AI for meeting coverage, internal conversations and cross-system reports rather than personally participating in every exchange. He presents trust in AI-mediated context as a difficult human adjustment, but one needed to keep pace with AI-enabled business activity. This is a recommended working pattern, not a demonstrated assurance of output reliability.
qs: To get there, you have to lean into not being in every conversation, but rather relying on AI to help you do that.

you need to trust that AI can have a quick conversation on Slack with someone to gather information for you, or it could sit in as the note taker on your meeting, or it could go run a quick report across several different business systems to help you gather context

kp.k: In-house pressure outpaces outside counsel efficiency gains
kp.d: Fleisher reports that GCs face faster-turnaround expectations and constrained hiring while generally seeing no change in outside counsel delivery times, billed hours or total costs despite claimed AI use. He recounts CEOs demanding business growth of three or four X without comparable legal headcount growth. He predicts pressure for alternative fee arrangements and cost or delivery improvements over the next year or two, rather than reporting that such changes have already occurred at scale.
qs: most GCs I talk to say that they ask their outside counsel about AI usage, and they say they’re using it, but they don’t see any change in either delivery times or actual billed hours and total cost.
We’re going to grow the business by three or four X this year, but you can’t grow legal, or you can only add one person.

I do think, though, that we are close to a breaking point where outside counsel will have to start offering more alternative fee arrangements and at least having some impact on either cost or time to deliver.
And so that will be an interesting one to watch play out over the next year or two.

kp.k: Current AI cannot replace legal staffing like-for-like
kp.d: Fleisher says internal staff and outside counsel historically dominate in-house spending, and current AI is not a direct substitute for junior lawyers, legal operations staff, paralegals or other non-lawyer roles. He warns that cutting legal budgets by 20% today would probably reduce work output by at least 10%. These figures are his illustrative prediction, not reported study results.
qs: There is some AI that maybe, at full scale, can really help you do the work that a junior lawyer can. But today, they are not like-for-like.
Even if you’re talking about legal ops and paralegals and non-lawyer roles, it’s still not at that level yet.
And so that, to me, is one of the core problems with saying, “Hey, let’s go cut legal’s budget today by 20%,” because you are probably going to see at least a 10% reduction in work output.

kp.k: Agentic workflows need not mean autonomous legal practice
kp.d: Fleisher distinguishes tools executing actions across systems from fully autonomous workflows. He characterizes internal context gathering as relatively low-risk, while recommending human approval for higher-risk actions such as counterparty negotiations and human review of resulting redlines. He says leading organizations generally retain these controls and regards fully autonomous end-to-end in-house workflows as distant or potentially unattainable.
qs: I think people generally think agent means autonomous, but it may not mean that. You can still have human-in-the-loop steps around the work that agents are doing.

If you have an agent that can send a Slack to someone to gather context and then take that and use it to improve a redline, that’s totally fine as long as that person you’re Slacking was expecting the message and you’re still signing off and reviewing the redline.
I think in those, you want to see more human-in-the-loop steps, where you have to press approve on anything that the agent is going to go do.

I think we are a very long way out, if not completely out, from in-house teams having fully autonomous tools that are going and completing end-to-end workflows without them touching them or being a human in the loop.

kp.k: Implementation combines workflow change, data curation and training
kp.d: Fleisher identifies changing established work habits as a major adoption obstacle, describing the potential removal of 30 or 40% of admin-intensive work rather than a measured saving. He says implementation requires cleaning data, extracting metadata and excluding irrelevant folders or outdated playbooks to avoid poor outputs and lost trust. Sandstone uses partners including LECG and internal former lawyers and legal operations leaders for embedded support and office hours; he also recalls teaching arbitrators AI's capabilities and limitations.
qs: I think the hardest thing that we see with getting people to adopt new tools is rewiring the way that they think about actually doing the work
Okay, I don't need to do this 30 or 40% of the work that is very admin-intensive. I can spend all my time focusing on the more complicated parts.
We use AI to help us clean it and improve it and extract valuable metadata.
If you don't do that upfront, you just get much worse outputs on the back end. And I think people don't trust the AI as much.
We do a lot of office hours, just teaching people what works and what doesn't.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nick Fleisher presents AI primarily as infrastructure for coordinating in-house legal work and augmenting lawyers, while predicting increased demand, budget pressure and eventual changes in outside-counsel delivery and pricing.
pts.d:
1. Context-integrated workflows: Fleisher says Sandstone centralizes requests from business systems, routes them, gathers business and counterparty context, and uses that material to assist drafting and review. Repeated use builds a department-wide knowledge layer connecting documents, people and companies. These are descriptions of his company's capabilities and intended development, not independently established performance findings.
2. Adoption differences: He says law firms adopted and invested in AI earlier, but their fragmented workflows and partner autonomy make organization-wide adoption difficult. In-house departments can obtain greater collective benefit when aligned around a common way of working; he identifies a gap between historical contract repositories and redlining point solutions.
3. Proactive legal departments: He argues that AI's value extends beyond cost savings to detecting forthcoming legal demand and capacity constraints before legal becomes a bottleneck. He reports clients using tools across business systems to anticipate work and prepare lower-level tasks or reconsider staffing.
4. Learning preferences and exposing differences: He says tools can progressively learn routing, approval and drafting preferences by observing work and collecting feedback. Comparing lawyers' decisions can expose habitual clause choices or assumptions about counterparties and help practitioners improve. His use of 'bias' here primarily concerns decision habits and differences within teams, rather than a claim that AI resolves social inequity.
5. Administrative automation before substantive substitution: He argues that lawyers should delegate administrative work, information retrieval and work allocation to AI rather than begin exclusively with harder tasks such as redlining. He reports some resistance to relinquishing administrative activities.
6. Limits to substitution: He predicts continuing human last-mile judgment, especially where legal risk must be weighed against business outcomes. He allows that some low-volume or low-stakes work, including lowest-value arbitration matters that might otherwise not be addressed, could be fully automated when the cost tradeoff warrants it. He does not predict that today's tools replace junior lawyers, legal operations staff or paralegals on a like-for-like basis.
7. More work rather than simply fewer hours: He says AI enables businesses to generate more agreements, negotiations and transactions and can also generate lower-quality material needing legal attention. Consequently, lawyers face additional volume and rework. He argues that they will need AI-mediated monitoring and information gathering to keep up rather than personally attend every conversation.
8. Pressure on in-house teams: He reports higher expectations for turnaround, restricted staffing growth and no corresponding, broadly visible improvement in outside-counsel prices or delivery times. He predicts that these pressures will force outside counsel toward more alternative fee arrangements and some reduction in cost or delivery time. He also warns that immediate budget cuts can reduce legal output because technology is not yet a direct labor substitute.
9. Agents with oversight: He describes current legal agents as systems that perform actions across tools, such as messaging employees for context and using it in a redline. He expects low-risk internal information-gathering agents to scale, while advocating approval steps for higher-risk external negotiations. Fully autonomous, end-to-end in-house workflows remain distant or may never arrive in his account.
10. Implementation determines value: He argues that relevant, organized data and workflow redesign are prerequisites for useful AI. Integrations, cleaning repositories, removing obsolete material, user education and hands-on implementation support are needed to turn tool purchases into value and maintain user trust.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Fleisher grounds his claims mainly in consulting experience, Sandstone implementation experience and conversations with general counsel; the transcript supplies no formal study, benchmark or independently measured productivity result.
pts.d: For claims 1–2, Fleisher describes his product and draws on work with large law firms and corporate legal departments at McKinsey. His comparison with engineering tools such as Linear and Jira is an analogy supporting his workflow-design argument. For claims 3–4, he reports observations of clients using proactive tools and learning decision preferences, but provides no named client case, sample size, quantified benefit or measurement protocol. The product-launch/capacity example and examples of clause habits and counterparty bargaining power illustrate mechanisms rather than document evaluated outcomes. For claims 5–6, he combines observed resistance to administrative change with his assessment of the difficulty of automating business-risk judgment; the boundary he draws around human decision-making is a prediction, not a demonstrated technical limit. For claim 7, he offers business observations and relays an unnamed GC's estimate of 30–40% more work associated with AI-generated material. That percentage is a second-hand anecdote, not Fleisher's measured market-wide increase. For claim 8, he reports conversations in which GCs see no change in outside-counsel delivery or bills despite reported AI use, and says he sees pressure with almost every client. His examples of business growth with constrained legal hiring are reported scenarios, not aggregate staffing data. His suggestion that a 20% legal budget cut would probably produce at least a 10% output reduction is an illustrative forecast without a disclosed calculation. For claim 9, he describes practices he says are the norm at leading organizations and makes a risk-based argument for oversight; no agent reliability or safety benchmark is supplied. For claim 10, he describes repository-cleaning problems, client feedback, implementation partnerships, an internal team of former lawyers and legal operations leaders, office hours, and experience teaching arbitrators what AI can and cannot do. These support an experience-based implementation argument without a controlled comparison. Claims are attributed here to Fleisher; hosts' separate assertions about courts and their own GC conversations are not treated as his evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview distinguishes current, imperfect augmentation in 2026 from gradual learning and implementation gains, a one-to-two-year outlook for outside-counsel change, and distant or uncertain full autonomy.
pts.d: Claims about current product functions, adoption challenges, client pressure, agents and implementation refer to the interview's 2026 setting. The integrated knowledge layer develops over time as more work passes through the system. Fleisher explicitly says preferences are not captured on day one: initial outputs will not fully resemble the lawyer's work, and the first couple of weeks may involve manual handling while the tool observes. Proactive value is conditional on successful adoption, access to relevant cross-business data, and willingness to rely on AI for information gathering. The two-week product-launch bottleneck is an illustrative forecast horizon inside a use case, not an implementation timetable. The prediction of rising legal workload is conditional in part on AI becoming as prevalent as anticipated across the business. Outside-counsel fee and delivery change is explicitly something to watch over the next year or two, approximately 2027–2028 from the 2026 interview, rather than an accomplished market transition. Fleisher says he has not yet seen such benefits materialize at scale. Labor substitution is similarly qualified: some AI might perform junior-lawyer work at full scale, but today's tools are not like-for-like replacements, including for non-lawyer roles. His broad prediction of continuing lawyer judgment is qualified by the possibility of full automation in some low-volume or low-stakes matters where economics justify it. For agents, internal context gathering is characterized as low risk, while external negotiation calls for human approval; redline use remains subject to human review and sign-off. He places fully autonomous end-to-end in-house workflows a very long way away, if achievable at all. Data cleanup and change management must precede or accompany deployment; no definite implementation duration or guaranteed productivity gain is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal, with implications for its business clients, outside counsel, implementation professionals and some low-value dispute work.
pts.d: In-house lawyers, particularly commercial lawyers handling sales and procurement contracts, are expected to spend less time collecting requests and context and more time on difficult legal decisions. Product counsel and department managers may gain earlier visibility of demand and capacity problems. GCs face simultaneous demands for faster delivery, more work and restrained spending or headcount. Business teams in sales, product and procurement interact with legal through existing systems and AI-mediated intake; Fleisher says their increased AI-enabled activity also generates additional legal volume and rework. Individual lawyers and their teams may have habitual decisions surfaced and compared, with potential learning benefits. Junior lawyers, paralegals and legal operations professionals are explicitly not presented as currently interchangeable with software; budget reductions based on that assumption risk lost output. Law firms, especially large firms with many partners, face collective-adoption difficulties and pressure from corporate buyers to translate AI use into improved delivery or alternative fees. Legal operations specialists, former lawyers and implementation partners are described as important to data preparation, workflow redesign and adoption. Sandstone is the software provider in this account, not an alternative legal service provider delivering the underlying legal work. Counterparties may be affected by negotiation agents, but Fleisher distinguishes that higher-risk external activity from internal information gathering and retains human approval. Participants in some lowest-value arbitration matters could receive automated handling where cost otherwise prevents work being undertaken; he does not establish a general access-to-justice outcome or quantify public benefit. Although he says data lessons apply across legal and draws an analogy to court backlogs, his concrete operational examples and observations focus on corporate legal departments rather than measured court transformation.
